{{Short description|Model particles in statistical mechanics}}
[[File:Tormaysala.svg|thumb|Orientations of two hard spheres in collision.]]

In [[statistical mechanics|statistical mechanics]], '''hard spheres''' are widely used as model particles in fluids and solids. They are defined simply as impenetrable spheres that cannot overlap in space. They mimic the extremely strong ("infinitely elastic bouncing") repulsion that atoms and spherical molecules experience at very close distances. Hard spheres systems are studied by analytical means, by [[molecular dynamics]] simulations, and by the experimental study of certain [[colloid]]al model systems.

Besides being a model of theoretical significance, the hard-sphere system is used as a basis in the formulation of several modern, predictive [[Equation of state|equations of state]] for real fluids through the [[statistical associating fluid theory]] (SAFT) approach, and models for transport properties in gases through [[Chapman–Enskog theory]].

==Formal definition==

Hard spheres of diameter <math>\sigma</math> are particles with the following pairwise interaction potential:

<math display="block">V(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2) = \begin{cases}
0      & \text{if} \quad |\mathbf{r}_1-\mathbf{r}_2| \geq \sigma \\
\infty & \text{if} \quad |\mathbf{r}_1-\mathbf{r}_2|  <   \sigma
\end{cases}</math>

where <math>\mathbf{r}_1</math> and <math>\mathbf{r}_2</math> are the positions of the two particles.

==Hard-spheres gas==

The first three [[virial coefficient]]s for hard spheres can be determined analytically

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{B_2}{v_0} &= 4 \\
\frac{B_3}{{v_0}^2} &= 10 \\
\frac{B_4}{{v_0}^3} &= -\frac{712}{35} + \frac{219 \sqrt{2}}{35 \pi}+\frac{4131}{35 \pi} \arccos{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}\approx 18.365
\end{align}</math> 

Higher-order ones can be determined numerically using [[Monte Carlo integration]]. We list

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{B_5}{{v_0}^4} &= 28.24 \pm 0.08 \\
\frac{B_6}{{v_0}^5} &= 39.5 \pm 0.4 \\
\frac{B_7}{{v_0}^6} &= 56.5 \pm 1.6
\end{align}</math>

A table of virial coefficients for up to eight dimensions can be found on the page [http://www.sklogwiki.org/SklogWiki/index.php/Hard_sphere:_virial_coefficients Hard sphere: virial coefficients].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Clisby |first1=Nathan |last2=McCoy |first2=Barry M. |title=Ninth and Tenth Order Virial Coefficients for Hard Spheres in D Dimensions |journal=Journal of Statistical Physics |date=January 2006 |volume=122 |issue=1 |pages=15–57 |doi=10.1007/s10955-005-8080-0|arxiv=cond-mat/0503525 |bibcode=2006JSP...122...15C |s2cid=16278678 }}</ref>

[[File:Hard-sphere phase diagram pressure packing fraction.svg|thumb|Phase diagram of hard sphere system (Solid line - stable branch, dashed line - metastable branch): Pressure <math>P</math> as a function of the volume fraction (or packing fraction) <math>\eta</math>]]

The hard sphere system exhibits a fluid-solid phase transition between the [[packing density|volume fractions]] of freezing <math>\eta_\mathrm{f}\approx 0.494</math> and melting <math>\eta_\mathrm{m} \approx 0.545</math>. The pressure diverges at [[random close pack]]ing <math>\eta_\mathrm{rcp}\approx 0.644</math> for the metastable liquid branch and at [[Close-packing of equal spheres|close packing]] <math>\eta_\mathrm{cp} = \sqrt{2}\pi/6 \approx 0.74048</math> for the stable solid branch.

==Hard-spheres liquid==

The [[static structure factor]] of the hard-spheres liquid can be calculated using the [[Percus–Yevick approximation]].

== Carnahan–Starling equation of state ==
A simple, yet popular [[equation of state]] describing systems of pure hard spheres was developed in 1969 by [[N. F. Carnahan|Norman F. Carnahan]] and [[K. E. Starling]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Carnahan |first=Norman F. |last2=Starling |first2=Kenneth E. |date=1969-07-15 |title=Equation of State for Nonattracting Rigid Spheres |url=https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1672048 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=51 |issue=2 |pages=635–636 |doi=10.1063/1.1672048 |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref> By expressing the compressibility of a hard-sphere system as a geometric series, the expression

<math display="block">Z = \frac{pV}{nRT} = \frac{1 + \eta + \eta^2 - \eta^3}{{\left(1 - \eta\right)}^3}</math>

is obtained, where <math>\eta</math> is the [[Packing density|packing fraction]], given by

<math display="block">\eta = \frac{N_A \pi n \sigma^3}{6V}</math>

where <math>N_A</math> is [[Avogadro constant|Avogadro's number]], <math>n / V</math> is the [[Molar concentration|molar density]] of the fluid, and <math>\sigma</math> is the diameter of the hard-spheres. From this Equation of State, one can obtain the [[Residual property (physics)|residual]] [[Helmholtz free energy|Helmholtz energy]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Lee |first=Lloyd L. |date=1995-12-01 |title=An accurate integral equation theory for hard spheres: Role of the zero-separation theorems in the closure relation |url=https://doi.org/10.1063/1.469998 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=103 |issue=21 |pages=9388–9396 |doi=10.1063/1.469998 |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

<math display="block">\frac{A_\text{res}}{nRT} =  \frac{4 \eta - 3 \eta^2}{{\left( 1 - \eta \right)}^2} ,</math>

which yields the [[Residual property (physics)|residual]] [[chemical potential]]

<math display="block">\frac{\mu_\text{res}}{RT} = \frac{8 \eta - 9 \eta^2 + 3 \eta^3}{{\left(1 - \eta\right)}^3}.</math>

One can also obtain the value of the [[radial distribution function]], <math>g(r)</math>, evaluated at the surface of a sphere,<ref name=":0" />

<math display="block">g(\sigma) = \frac{1 - \frac{1}{2} \eta}{{\left(1 - \eta\right)}^3}.</math>

The latter is of significant importance to accurate descriptions of more advanced intermolecular potentials based on [[perturbation theory]], such as [[Statistical associating fluid theory|SAFT]], where a system of hard spheres is taken as a reference system, and the complete [[Pair potential|pair-potential]] is described by perturbations to the underlying hard-sphere system. Computation of the transport properties of hard-sphere gases at moderate densities using [[revised Enskog theory]] also relies on an accurate value for <math>g(\sigma)</math>, and the Carnahan–Starling equation of state has been used for this purpose to large success.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=López de Haro |first=M. |last2=Cohen |first2=E. G. D. |last3=Kincaid |first3=J. M. |date=1983-03-01 |title=The Enskog theory for multicomponent mixtures. I. Linear transport theory |url=https://doi.org/10.1063/1.444985 |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=78 |issue=5 |pages=2746–2759 |doi=10.1063/1.444985 |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
